title: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
summary: Why open-ended output is hard to score, where BLEU, ROUGE and BERTScore fail, judge biases and fixes, Bradley-Terry ratings, human agreement, and paired bootstrap significance.
outcomes: Compute BLEU and ROUGE for a candidate and explain, with published evidence, why overlap metrics misjudge correct paraphrases
Explain position, verbosity and self-preference bias in LLM judges and apply swap, length-control and judge-separation fixes
Fit a Bradley-Terry rating from pairwise votes and explain why online Elo depends on vote order
Design a blind pairwise human study and compute Cohen's kappa for three-way preference labels
Build a task-specific regression suite and compute a paired bootstrap confidence interval for a score change

lessons.title: Why open-ended output is hard to score

blocks.md:
In search evaluation the system picks from a fixed set of documents, and a label says how relevant each one is. A generator instead writes **new text**: a summary, an answer, a reply. There is no fixed list of candidates to label in advance, and many different outputs can be equally good.

Quality also has several dimensions at once: is it **correct** and faithful to the sources, **complete**, **helpful** for this user, in the right **format** and tone, and **safe**? One number rarely captures all of them.

Liu et al. (EMNLP 2016) give a compact example from dialogue. The context is "Hey John, what do you want to do tonight?" then "Why don't we go see a movie?". The reference reply is "Nah, I hate that stuff, let's do something active." A model replies "Oh sure! Heard the film about Turing is out!", a perfectly reasonable answer that shares no words with the reference, so its BLEU score is 0.

Any evaluator that compares to one reference punishes valid diversity. Evaluators that do not use a reference must instead understand the task, which brings its own errors.

blocks.title: The main families of generation evaluators

scenes.caption: When the task has a checkable answer (code that must pass tests, a number, a label), use the check. It is cheap and exact. Open-ended text usually lacks one.
Reference metrics compare the output with one or more human-written references. Cheap and repeatable, but they need references and reward surface overlap.
An LLM judge reads the output (and maybe a reference or rubric) and grades it or picks the better of two. Scalable, but it has known biases.
Every automatic evaluator is only trusted after checking it against careful human judgments on your task, which themselves approximate what users want.

blocks.md: Keep two levels apart. **Segment level** asks whether a metric ranks individual outputs the way people do. **System level** asks whether it ranks whole systems (averaged over a test set) the way people do. Novikova et al. (EMNLP 2017) compared 21 automatic metrics on end-to-end NLG systems and found they only weakly reflect human judgments of individual outputs, while being more reliable at the system level. Averaging cancels some noise, which is why a metric can be useless for spotting a bad answer yet still roughly order two systems.

An evaluator is a measuring instrument. Before trusting any number it produces, check how often it agrees with careful human judgment on your task, at the level (single output or whole system) at which you will use it.

blocks.question: Why is an open-ended task such as summarization harder to score than a classification task?
options: Summaries are longer, so metrics run slower
Many different outputs can be equally good, so there is no single correct answer to compare against
Classification has no notion of quality
Summaries cannot be read by humans reliably
blocks.explain: With classification, one label is correct and a match check suffices. With open-ended text, the space of valid outputs is huge, so overlap with one reference is a weak proxy and a judge must actually understand the content.

blocks.question: A metric correlates poorly with human ratings of single responses but orders five systems the same way humans do. How should you use it?
options: Use it to flag individual bad responses in production
Never use it for anything
Use it, with care, to compare whole systems on a test set, not to judge single outputs
Use it only on outputs shorter than the reference
blocks.explain: Novikova et al. found the same pattern: metrics are more reliable at the system level than at the segment level, because averaging over many outputs cancels some per-output errors.

lessons.title: BLEU, ROUGE and BERTScore, and where they fail

blocks.md: **BLEU** (Papineni et al., ACL 2002) was built for machine translation. It counts how many of the candidate's n-grams (runs of n words, for n = 1 to 4) appear in the reference. Counts are **clipped**: a word only matches as many times as it occurs in the reference, so repeating "the" cannot inflate the score. The four precisions are combined with a geometric mean, and a **brevity penalty** stops very short candidates from scoring high precision by saying little.

blocks.caption: p_n is the clipped n-gram precision, c the candidate length and r the reference length. Scores are usually computed over a whole test corpus.

blocks.md: **ROUGE** (Lin, 2004) was built for summarization and is recall-oriented. ROUGE-N is the fraction of the reference's n-grams that appear in the candidate. ROUGE-L uses the **longest common subsequence**: the longest sequence of words that appears in both texts in the same order, not necessarily adjacent.

blocks.prompt: Reference: "the demo was moved to friday since the lead is sick". Candidate A: "as the lead is ill the demo is now on friday" (correct). Candidate B: "the demo was moved to monday since the lead is sick" (wrong day). Which scores higher on BLEU and ROUGE?
blocks.reveal: B, by a wide margin. B shares 10 of 11 words in the same order, so overlap metrics love it even though its single changed word makes it wrong. A carries the right meaning in different words and is punished. The figure below computes the numbers.

scenes.caption: Two candidates of 11 words each against one 11-word reference.
A: 6 of 11 words match after clipping (the second "is" is clipped, since the reference has only one). Unigram precision 6/11 = 0.545.
B: 10 of 11 words match. The only miss is the word that makes B wrong: monday. Unigram precision 10/11 = 0.909.
Longer n-grams widen the gap. A shares only "the lead is" as a trigram and no 4-gram; B keeps 4 of 8 four-grams because the error sits in the middle.

blocks.title: Overlap metrics for the two candidates

scenes.caption: Candidate A (correct paraphrase). Sentence BLEU is exactly 0 because the 4-gram precision is 0 and the geometric mean multiplies it in. This is why sentence-level BLEU needs smoothing and BLEU is meant for corpora.
Candidate B (wrong day): BLEU 0.702, ROUGE-1 0.909, ROUGE-2 0.8, ROUGE-L 0.909. Every overlap metric prefers the wrong answer.

blocks.md: BLEU is also not one number. Post (WMT 2018, [A Call for Clarity in Reporting BLEU Scores](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.08771)) found differences as high as 1.8 BLEU between commonly used configurations of the same metric, mainly from how the reference is tokenized and normalized, and released SacreBLEU so papers report one standard configuration with a version signature.

**BERTScore** (Zhang et al., ICLR 2020) replaces exact matching with similarity of contextual embeddings. Each token in the reference is matched to its most similar token in the candidate (greedy matching by cosine similarity), and vice versa. Recall averages the best match of each reference token; precision averages the best match of each candidate token; F1 combines them. Optional idf weighting gives rare words more weight, and baseline rescaling spreads the scores over a more readable range.

blocks.caption: x is the reference, x-hat the candidate; token embeddings are normalized, so the dot product is the cosine similarity.

scenes.caption: Cosine similarity between each reference token and each candidate token. Simplified: hand-made 3-dimensional toy vectors, not real BERT embeddings.
Recall: for each reference row take the best match. "sick" matches "ill" at 0.99 even though the strings differ. R = (1.0 + 1.0 + 0.99) / 3 = 0.997.
Precision does the same per candidate column; here it is also 0.997. Exact-match ROUGE-1 for this pair would be 2/3, because "ill" is not "sick".

blocks.md:
Soft matching fixes paraphrase, but it does not check facts. In the same toy space, "monday" and "friday" have cosine 0.99: words that play the same role often sit close together, so a swapped entity can cost very little.

The evidence across tasks:

- **Dialogue** (Liu et al. 2016): on Twitter, BLEU-2's Spearman correlation with human ratings was 0.36 and ROUGE's 0.12; on Ubuntu technical chat they were 0.04 and 0.05, while two halves of the human raters correlated at 0.95 and 0.96.
- **Summarization** (Goyal et al. 2022): people overwhelmingly preferred GPT-3 summaries, yet those scored more than 7 ROUGE-L points below a fine-tuned model, lower even than the trivial Lead-3 baseline in prior work. BERTScore and QA-based metrics also failed to reflect the preference.
- **Translation** (Kocmi et al. 2021, Microsoft): over 3,344 pairs of MT systems with human judgments, the chart below shows how often each metric picked the same winner as humans.

blocks.title: Agreement with humans on which MT system is better (Kocmi et al.)

scenes.caption: Accuracy over all 3,344 system pairs. String overlap metrics (BLEU, ChrF) sit near 75%.
Pretrained metrics do better, and COMET, which is trained on human quality judgments, leads at 83.4%. The authors recommend a pretrained metric such as COMET as primary and advise against BLEU.

blocks.md: Overlap metrics measure closeness to a reference, not correctness. A fluent answer with one wrong fact can outscore a correct paraphrase. They also penalize outputs that are better than, but different from, the reference, which is common once a strong LLM writes the outputs.

blocks.question: You switch your summarizer from a fine-tuned model to a prompted LLM. ROUGE-L drops by 7 points. What should you conclude?
options: The new summarizer is clearly worse
Nothing yet: run a human or validated-judge comparison, because ROUGE penalizes summaries that differ in style from the references
ROUGE-L must be replaced by ROUGE-1
The references are wrong and should be deleted
blocks.explain: Goyal et al. saw exactly this: GPT-3 summaries scored over 7 ROUGE-L points lower than a fine-tuned model while people strongly preferred them. The fine-tuned model was trained to imitate the reference style, which overlap metrics reward.

blocks.question: In the BERTScore toy, the reference token "sick" and candidate token "ill" have similarity 0.99. Which statement is true?
options: BERTScore recall counts "sick" as fully unmatched
BERTScore requires the candidate and reference to have equal length
BERTScore is identical to ROUGE-1 when idf weighting is off
BERTScore gives partial credit for paraphrases, but it would also give near-full credit to many factual swaps
blocks.explain: Greedy embedding matching rewards meaning-similar words, fixing the paraphrase problem. It does not verify facts, and words of the same type (weekdays, names, numbers) can be close in embedding space.

lessons.title: LLM judges for generation: modes, biases and fixes

blocks.md:
The LLM-as-judge course showed how to prompt a model to label relevance, measure its agreement with humans, and fix position bias by judging both orders and counting inconsistent verdicts as ties. For open-ended generation the same tool is used in three modes described by Zheng et al. (MT-Bench):

- **Pairwise comparison**: which of two answers is better (or a tie).
- **Single-answer grading**: a score, say 1 to 10, for one answer, ideally against an explicit rubric.
- **Reference-guided grading**: the judge also sees a reference answer, which helps on math and reasoning where judges otherwise miss errors.

This lesson goes deeper on the three biases that matter most for generation and on fixes with published evidence.

**Position bias.** Wang et al. (2023) showed how far it can go: with ChatGPT as the evaluator, Vicuna-13B could be made to beat ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries just by changing the order in which the two answers appear. Their fixes:

1. **Balanced Position Calibration**: evaluate in both orders and average the scores.
2. **Multiple Evidence Calibration**: make the judge write its evidence (explanation) before the score, and sample several judgments.
3. **Human-in-the-loop Calibration**: route items where verdicts vary most across orders to people.

**Verbosity bias.** Judges tend to prefer longer answers. Dubois et al. ([Length-Controlled AlpacaEval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.04475)) measured how gameable the AlpacaEval benchmark was: by only asking the baseline model (`gpt4_1106_preview`) to be more concise or more detailed, its win rate ranged from 22.9% to 64.3%.

Their fix is a regression. They fit a logistic model of the judge's preference with a model term, an instruction-difficulty term, and a **length term**: a coefficient times $\tanh$ of the standardized length difference. The **length-controlled win rate** is the model's prediction with the length term set to zero, answering "what would the judge prefer if both answers had the same length?"

blocks.caption: Length-controlled AlpacaEval's GLM (Dubois et al., Eq. 1). sigma is the logistic function; dropping the tanh term gives the length-controlled preference.

blocks.title: How a length term shifts a judge's preference

scenes.caption: Two equally good models (quality gap 0). With a length weight of 1, the longer one wins about 68% of comparisons when it is 1 std longer. Simplified: parameters are illustrative, not fitted values.
A slightly better model (gap 0.3) that writes shorter answers loses at negative length differences. The length-controlled curve still shows its true edge, about 57%.
With no length effect (phi = 0) the curves coincide. The regression estimates phi from data instead of assuming it.

blocks.title: Win-rate range when only verbosity is changed (Dubois et al.)

scenes.caption: Raw AlpacaEval: the same baseline model ranges from 22.9% to 64.3% when only prompted to be concise or verbose.
Length-controlled: 41.9% to 51.6%. The correction also raised AlpacaEval's Spearman correlation with Chatbot Arena from 0.94 to 0.98.

blocks.md:
**Self-preference.** A judge may favour text written by itself. In MT-Bench, Zheng et al. saw hints of this but could not establish it. Panickssery et al. (2024) went further: GPT-4 and Llama 2 can tell their own outputs from others' with non-trivial accuracy out of the box, and when they fine-tuned models, self-preference strength rose linearly with self-recognition ability.

The practical fix is separation: use a judge from a different model family from the systems being compared, as Anthropic's evaluation guide also advises ("evaluate with a different model from the one used to generate the evaluated output"), and check the judge on a human-labelled subset that includes outputs from each system.

A safe default for generation judging: pairwise or rubric grading with the explanation before the verdict; both orders, with disagreement treated as a tie; report and control length; a judge outside the model families being compared; and a human-labelled subset to measure agreement before every major change.

blocks.question: Your new prompt makes answers about twice as long, and your LLM judge's pairwise win rate jumps from 50% to 68%. What is the best next step?
options: Ship it: 68% is a clear win
Check whether the gain survives at matched length, for example with a length-controlled regression or a human review of a sample
Switch the judge to single-answer grading, which has no length bias
Shorten the old answers by truncation and re-run
blocks.explain: Dubois et al. showed verbosity alone can move a win rate by tens of points. Estimate the preference at equal length (or ask people) before attributing the gain to quality. Single-answer grading is not immune to length bias, and truncation damages the baseline.

blocks.question: Which mitigation targets position bias specifically?
options: Using a judge from a different model family
Fitting a tanh length term
Evaluating both orders and combining the results
Adding a reference answer to the prompt
blocks.explain: Balanced Position Calibration (Wang et al.) and swap-and-tie (Zheng et al.) run both orders so that position effects cancel or show up as ties. A different-family judge targets self-preference; the length term targets verbosity.

blocks.question: You compare your fine-tuned model against a competitor, using the base model of your fine-tune as the judge. Your model wins 61%. Which concern is most specific to this setup?
options: Self-preference: the judge may recognise and favour text that resembles its own outputs
Position bias cannot occur in this setup
The judge is too small to read both answers
Pairwise comparisons cannot produce win rates above 60%
blocks.explain: Panickssery et al. linked self-recognition to self-preference. A judge closely related to one contestant is not neutral. Re-judge with an unrelated model family and validate on human labels.

lessons.title: Pairwise preference, Elo and Bradley-Terry ratings

blocks.md:
Saying which of two answers is better is easier than giving an absolute grade, and it sidesteps disagreements about what a 7 out of 10 means. **Chatbot Arena** (Chiang et al., 2024) is the best-known system built on this. A user writes a prompt, two anonymous models answer side by side, and the user votes for one, a tie, or both bad; the names are revealed only after the vote. The paper reports over 240K votes from about 90K users covering more than 50 models.

Thousands of pairwise votes then have to become one rating per model.

The **Elo** system from chess updates ratings online, after every game. With ratings $R_A$ and $R_B$, A's expected score is below; after the game, A's rating moves by $K$ times (actual minus expected), where the actual score is 1 for a win, 0.5 for a tie and 0 for a loss. Two models at 1000 each expect 0.5, so with $K = 32$ the winner gains 16 points.

blocks.tex: E_A = \frac{1}{1 + 10^{(R_B - R_A)/400}}, \qquad R_A \leftarrow R_A + K\,(S_A - E_A)
blocks.caption: Standard Elo expected score and update. K controls how much one game moves the rating.

blocks.md: The Arena team found [considerable variability](https://lmsys.org/blog/2023-12-07-leaderboard/) in online Elo ratings and moved to the **Bradley-Terry (BT)** model, which assumes each model has a fixed strength and fits all votes at once by maximum likelihood (a logistic regression). Their blog counts ties as half a win and half a loss. The Arena paper says BT coefficients are "better for the purpose of statistical estimation".

blocks.caption: BT win probability (Arena paper, Eq. 2). Multiplying the strengths xi by 400/ln 10 puts them on the familiar Elo scale; the 1000 offset is an arbitrary anchor (here, the mean).

blocks.md: A toy with three models and 60 votes (ties dropped): A beat B 14 to 6, A beat C 16 to 4, and B beat C 12 to 8. A script fits BT by maximum likelihood and also runs online Elo ($K = 32$, start at 1000) over the same 60 votes in different orders.

scenes.caption: Bradley-Terry fit: A 1128.7, B 974.1, C 897.3. Its predicted win rates (A over B 0.709, A over C 0.791, B over C 0.609) closely match the observed 0.70, 0.80, 0.60.
Online Elo, order 1: all 12 of C's wins arrive last. C ends on top at 1051.7, ahead of A at 990.2. Recent games dominate.
Online Elo, order 2: C's wins arrive first. Now C is last at 838.6 and B (1081.3) edges out A (1080.1). Same votes, opposite story.
Averaging online Elo over 1,000 random orders gives 1117.5, 976.1, 906.4, close to BT. BT gets there directly because it ignores order by design.

blocks.md:
A rating needs an uncertainty. The Arena paper builds confidence intervals for the BT coefficients (it considered the bootstrap and "sandwich" robust standard errors, and deploys the latter) and derives a rank for each model as 1 plus the number of models whose lower bound is above its upper bound. Ties in rank are allowed.

Below, a script bootstraps our toy: resample the 60 votes with replacement 1,000 times, refit BT each time, and take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. It then repeats the exercise with 360 votes in the same proportions.

blocks.title: 95% bootstrap intervals for BT ratings (axis: rating minus 800)

scenes.caption: 60 votes: A 1059 to 1228, B 882 to 1047, C 805 to 972. A's lower bound is above B's upper bound, so A ranks 1. B and C overlap, so both rank 2.
360 votes with the same win proportions: A 1099 to 1166, B 941 to 1004, C 866 to 927. Intervals are about 2.5 times narrower, none overlap, and the ranks become 1, 2, 3.

blocks.md:
How good are crowd votes? The Arena paper compared crowd votes with two expert graders on sampled battles: crowd and experts agreed 72.8% to 83.1% of the time, the two experts agreed 79.4% to 89.8%, and a GPT-4 judge agreed with the experts 76.3% to 81.0%. Crowd preference is noisy but not far from expert disagreement.

Two caveats for your own use. A public arena's prompts come from its visitors, so its ranking describes that prompt distribution, not your product's. And a preference vote reflects everything a voter likes about an answer, not only its correctness, so validate it against the criteria your product cares about.

Do not rank by raw win percentage when models faced different opponents: beating weak models inflates it. BT accounts for who played whom. And never report a ranking without intervals; with few votes, neighbouring models are often statistically tied.

blocks.question: Why did Chatbot Arena move from online Elo to Bradley-Terry?
options: Elo cannot handle more than two models
BT needs fewer votes because it ignores ties
Elo ratings cannot be shown on a 400-point scale
Online Elo depends on vote order and favours recent games; BT fits all votes at once assuming fixed strengths, giving stabler estimates and better intervals
blocks.explain: The toy showed it: the same 60 votes gave opposite Elo rankings in different orders. The LMSYS blog cites variability in the online algorithm and describes BT as the maximum likelihood estimate of the underlying Elo model.

blocks.question: Model X beats model Y in 60% of head-to-head votes. Roughly how far apart are they on the Elo-style BT scale?
options: About 20 points
About 70 points
About 200 points
About 400 points
blocks.explain: The BT logit gap is ln(0.6/0.4) = 0.405. Multiplying by 400/ln 10 = 173.7 gives about 70 points. A 400-point gap would mean about a 91% win rate.

blocks.question: Two models' 95% rating intervals overlap substantially. What should a leaderboard say?
options: They share a rank: the data cannot separate them yet
The one with the higher point estimate is better
The one with fewer votes is better
Drop the model with the wider interval
blocks.explain: Following the Arena rank rule, a model is only ranked below another when the other's lower bound exceeds its upper bound. Overlap means more votes are needed before claiming an order.

lessons.title: Designing human evaluations and measuring agreement

blocks.md:
Every automatic evaluator in this course is checked against people, so the human evaluation itself must be trustworthy. The main design choices:

- **Pairwise or absolute.** Pairwise ("which is better, or tie?") is easier to answer consistently and directly gives a win rate; absolute scales (1 to 5 per criterion) give scores you can track over time but drift between annotators.
- **One criterion at a time.** Ask separately about correctness, completeness and tone, or say which dominates; a single "overall quality" invites each annotator to weigh them differently.
- **Blind and randomized.** Hide which system wrote which answer (Chatbot Arena reveals model names only after the vote), and randomize which side each system appears on.
- **Guidelines with examples**, including what counts as a tie and how to treat an answer that is both fluent and wrong.
- **Overlap.** Have at least two people label a shared subset so you can measure agreement before trusting the rest.

blocks.title: A human preference study with an agreement gate

nodes.label:
Outputs from
systems A and B

scenes.caption: Sample prompts from the traffic you care about and generate both systems' answers.
Strip system names and randomize which answer is on the left, so neither identity nor position can sway the vote.
Measure agreement on the overlap subset first. Low agreement means the task or guidelines are ambiguous, not that one annotator is wrong.
Only when agreement is acceptable do you aggregate labels into a win rate, with a confidence interval (lesson 6).

blocks.md:
The agreement statistic is **Cohen's kappa**, which you computed in the LLM-as-judge course: $\kappa = (p_o - p_e)/(1 - p_e)$, observed agreement corrected by the agreement two annotators would reach by chance given how often each uses each label. Here it is applied to a pairwise study with three labels: **A** better, **tie**, **B** better.

Two annotators labelled the same 20 answer pairs. Annotator 1 used A 8 times, tie 5 and B 7; annotator 2 used A 8, tie 4 and B 8.

blocks.title: Two annotators on 20 pairs (rows annotator 1, columns annotator 2)

scenes.caption: Observed counts. Row sums 8, 5, 7 and column sums 8, 4, 8 are each annotator's label frequencies.
Agreements on the diagonal: 6 + 2 + 5 = 13 of 20, so p_o = 0.65.
Expected counts if both labelled at random with their own frequencies: row sum x column sum / 20. The diagonal sums to 3.2 + 1.0 + 2.8 = 7, so p_e = 7/20 = 0.35.
Back to observed counts. Of the 7 disagreements, 5 involve a tie; only 2 are outright flips (A versus B). Among the 13 pairs where both picked a side, they agreed on 11.

blocks.caption: Computed by script from the confusion matrix above. Agreement is 65%, but less than half of the possible improvement over chance is realised.

blocks.md:
What to do with a kappa of 0.46 depends on where the disagreements are. Here they cluster on the tie label, which points at the guideline, not the annotators: one person calls "both fine, slightly different style" a tie, the other picks a side. A written tie rule (for example, "tie only when neither answer has an error and the differences are stylistic") plus a short calibration round on examples is the usual fix, followed by a fresh overlap sample to re-measure.

Experts disagree too. In the Chatbot Arena study, two expert graders agreed on 79.4% to 89.8% of sampled battles, so a target of perfect agreement is unrealistic for open-ended preference.
Do not report raw percent agreement alone. With skewed labels (say 90% of pairs are ties) two annotators agree often by chance. Report kappa with the confusion matrix, and say how ties were handled.

blocks.question: Two annotators reach observed agreement 0.80 on a pairwise study where chance agreement is 0.50. What is Cohen's kappa?
In the toy, 5 of 7 disagreements involve the tie label. Which change most directly targets that?
options: Hire annotators who never use ties
Write an explicit tie rule with examples, run a calibration round, then re-measure kappa on a fresh overlap sample
Drop all pairs that any annotator called a tie, then report kappa on the rest
Switch to a 1 to 10 scale
blocks.explain: The disagreement is about what a tie means, which is a guideline problem. Dropping ties after the fact inflates agreement and biases the win rate; forbidding ties forces random picks on truly equal pairs.

lessons.title: Task-specific eval sets, regression tests and significance

blocks.md:
Public benchmarks rarely match your product. A **task-specific eval set** is a list of inputs from your own task, each with what a good output must do: an exact answer, a checkable property, or a rubric for a judge. Build it like this:

1. **Sample real traffic** (logs, support tickets), stratified so each important slice (intent, language, length, customer tier) is represented.
2. **Add edge cases on purpose.** Anthropic's evaluation guide lists irrelevant or nonexistent input, overly long input, harmful input, and ambiguous cases where even humans would disagree.
3. **Prefer automatic grading** where possible (code checks, string match, a validated judge). The same guide puts it bluntly: "More questions with slightly lower signal automated grading is better than fewer questions with high-quality human hand-graded evals."
4. **Freeze a test portion** that you do not look at while iterating, as in prompt optimization.

A **regression test** runs the whole eval set on every change: a new prompt, model version, retriever or temperature. Because both versions see the same items, compare them **per item**: which items went from pass to fail, which from fail to pass, and how each slice moved. A small average gain can hide a broken slice.

blocks.title: An eval suite as a regression gate

nodes.label:
Run old and new
on every item

Paired bootstrap
CI on the delta

scenes.caption: Every change runs against the same frozen eval set, old and new side by side.
Graders score each output. Per-item results make the comparison paired: the same input, two versions.
The overall delta gets a confidence interval. A release decision uses the interval and the slices, not just the point estimate.

blocks.md: A worked example, computed by a script. Old and new prompts are graded pass or fail on the same **50 items**. Old passes 34 (0.68), new passes 39 (0.78): a gain of **+0.10**. Per item: both pass on 31, only new passes on 8, only old passes on 3, both fail on 8.

blocks.prompt: Is a 10-point gain on 50 items enough to claim the new prompt is better?
blocks.reveal: Not on its own. Only 11 items changed outcome (8 improved, 3 got worse); the other 39 tell you nothing about the difference. Resampling those items shows the gain could plausibly be zero or negative. The bootstrap below quantifies it.

blocks.md: The **paired bootstrap** (used for MT significance since Koehn, EMNLP 2004): draw 50 items with replacement from the 50, recompute new minus old on that resample, repeat 10,000 times, and read the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles as a 95% confidence interval. Resampling **items**, with both systems' results kept together, is what makes it paired.

blocks.code:
import random

def paired_bootstrap(old, new, B=10_000, seed=0):
    """old, new: per-item scores on the same items, in the same order."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    n = len(old)
    deltas = []
    for _ in range(B):
        idx = [rng.randrange(n) for _ in range(n)]
        deltas.append(sum(new[i] - old[i] for i in idx) / n)
    deltas.sort()
    return deltas[int(0.025 * B)], deltas[int(0.975 * B) - 1]
blocks.caption: Paired bootstrap confidence interval for the difference in mean score.

scenes.caption: Distribution of the resampled gain. It centres on the observed +0.10 but is wide, because only 11 items differ between the versions.
809 of 10,000 resamples (8.1%) show no gain or a loss. The 95% interval is -0.02 to +0.22: it includes zero, so the evidence is not conclusive.

blocks.md:
Two comparisons from the same script:

- **Unpaired** bootstrap (resampling each version's scores independently) gives -0.08 to +0.28, much wider. It throws away the fact that the same items are easy or hard for both versions.
- With **400 items** in the same proportions, the paired interval is +0.055 to +0.145: now clearly above zero.

The width shrinks with $\sqrt{n}$. A normal approximation makes the trade-off easy to plan: the half-width is about $1.96\, s_d / \sqrt{n}$, where $s_d$ is the standard deviation of the per-item difference (0.46 here).

blocks.title: 95% CI half-width for a paired difference

scenes.caption: With s = 0.46, 50 items give a half-width near 0.13 and 400 items near 0.045. Detecting a 3-point change needs about (1.96 x 0.46 / 0.03) squared = 903 items.
If the two versions differ on fewer items (more ties per item), s drops. At s = 0.3 the same precision needs far fewer items. Paired designs help exactly by lowering s.

blocks.md: Kocmi et al. reached the same conclusion for machine translation: alongside choosing a better metric, they recommend running a paired significance test before claiming one system beats another. And if you compare many variants against one baseline, some will look significant by luck; correct for multiple comparisons or confirm the winner on fresh items.

Report a gain as an interval, computed by resampling items with both systems paired. If the interval includes zero, say "not distinguishable on this set" and either add items or keep the old version. Check slices as well as the average.

blocks.question: Your paired bootstrap 95% interval for new minus old is -0.01 to +0.15. What is the correct summary?
options: The new version is 7 points better
The new version is worse
The data are consistent with no improvement; the eval set is too small to separate them
The bootstrap failed because the interval is not symmetric
blocks.explain: An interval that includes zero means you cannot rule out no difference at the 95% level. Add items, or treat the change as unproven. Bootstrap intervals need not be symmetric.

blocks.question: Why is the paired interval (-0.02 to +0.22) narrower than the unpaired one (-0.08 to +0.28) on the same data?
options: Pairing uses more resamples
Pairing keeps each item's old and new result together, so item difficulty, which affects both versions, cancels out of the difference
The unpaired method has a bug
Pairing drops the items where both versions pass
blocks.explain: Most items are easy or hard for both versions. Resampling them together removes that shared variation from the difference; resampling separately adds it back as noise.

blocks.question: You want to detect a 2-point change in pass rate, and the per-item difference has standard deviation about 0.4. Roughly how many items do you need for a 95% half-width of 0.02?
options: About 160
About 400
About 1,500
About 10,000
blocks.explain: n is about (1.96 x 0.4 / 0.02) squared = 39.2 squared, about 1,537 items. Small eval sets can only detect large changes.
